intro: Sixteen concepts connecting people, knowledge production and the transformation of systems. Each is defined, related to my approach and supported by scientific or institutional references in APA format.

autodetermination: Being an agent in one’s own life: choosing, deciding and pursuing personally meaningful goals. This requires real opportunities for choice, recognition of preferences and support adapted to the person’s capabilities and circumstances.
In educational support and reflection on where people live, supporting their preferences and their ability to act.
Wehmeyer’s functional model describes self-determined behaviour; Ryan and Deci’s theory addresses motivation and the needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness.
pouvoir: Developing a person’s or community’s real ability to act on what matters to them. This process connects skills, resources, rights, recognition and access to decision-making spaces.
Designing tools that preserve users’ choices and examining the social and organisational barriers that restrict those choices.
Empowerment has individual, collective and structural dimensions; access to resources matters alongside personal dispositions.
participation: Involving people in the questions and decisions that concern them, with the means to contribute: understandable information, time, accessibility and recognition. Their influence may extend to identifying needs, considering options, making choices and evaluation.
In partnership work, specifying who participates, when, and how their contributions influence decisions.
Consultation, collaboration and shared decision-making involve different degrees of influence. Making that influence explicit helps establish the scope of participation.
equite: Creating fairer conditions for accessing resources, participation and health, taking needs and barriers into account. Equity addresses avoidable and unjust disadvantages that hinder people’s ability to realise their capabilities and aspirations.
In my values and public health reflections, considering the social conditions and support that make genuine choice possible.
Different forms of support may be needed to enable everyone to exercise their capabilities and pursue their choices.
faireavec: Developing support and action with the person: connecting what they want to do, what they can do and the support available. Professionals contribute a framework, resources and expertise that make participation possible.
In specialised educational support and learning tools, developing approaches that people can understand, adjust and make their own.
Support retains a professional framework and adapts to the person’s autonomy, responsibilities and situational constraints.
coconstruction: Developing a project, tool or knowledge together across several stages: framing the problem, choosing options, producing, interpreting and evaluating. Cooperation benefits from explicit roles and decision-making arrangements.
A guiding principle for developing tools and preparing research workshops around the needs of the people concerned.
Its quality depends on shared power, recognition of contributions and the resources needed to participate.
experientiels: Knowledge developed through lived experience and making sense of it: illness, disability, support, everyday life or service use. It offers situated insight into how arrangements are used, the difficulties encountered and their practical effects.
Recognising the expertise of people concerned alongside professional and scientific knowledge in care, teaching and research.
An individual experience illuminates a context; collective discussion and combining knowledge sources help clarify its scope and limits.
epistemique: In my ongoing work, this term describes experience and the consequences of action feeding back into knowledge frameworks: practice can prompt reconsideration of categories, indicators and decision-making rules.
The manuscript presented under Research areas explores this movement from practice back towards knowledge and public health governance.
Here it is a research proposition under development, distinct from simply disseminating or returning findings. The references below illuminate its theoretical foundations.
systemie: Understanding phenomena through interactions between people, organisations, institutions and environments. Interdependence, feedback loops and delays help explain how a local action may produce effects at several levels.
In my thesis, connecting social needs, networks around CLSCs and the rules that organise different actors’ responses.
A systems perspective leads to hypotheses about mechanisms and then to documenting relationships and anticipated or observed effects.
intersectorialite: Organising cooperation between different sectors around shared needs and determinants: health, housing, social services, education or community action. Common goals, explicit roles and coordination arrangements support this response.
A central concept in my thesis: studying how several sectors respond to complex, co-occurring social needs, starting from CLSCs.
It involves negotiating priorities, responsibilities and resources between sectors, beyond professionals simply working near one another.
integration: Connecting professional and organisational interventions into a continuous, understandable pathway centred on people’s needs. Integration operates at clinical, professional, organisational and system levels.
Connecting local services, transitions between organisations and the conditions supporting independent living at home.
Shared supports, including information, goals and coordination arrangements, connect these different levels of integration.
implantation: Organising change in a particular setting by addressing adoption conditions, adaptation, available resources and evaluation. The CFIR helps examine factors that enable or impede implementation.
For proposals arising from research, examining roles, resources and local constraints before considering deployment.
A determinant framework helps explain context; a theory, a process model and an evaluation approach serve different functions.
resilience: A process of adaptation and rebuilding in the face of adversity, supported by personal, relational, social and institutional resources. Its form depends on people’s histories, environments and opportunities for support.
In my own path, turning hardships into resources while recognising the collective conditions that make rebuilding possible.
Resilience varies with circumstances and accessible resources. It does not justify leaving individuals to compensate for inequalities on their own.
reflexivite: Examining how one’s position, experience, values and choices shape questions, relationships and interpretations. This makes influences open to discussion and allows choices to be revised as work develops.
In my research stance, the reflective journal planned in the protocol and reflection on my use of AI, particularly in PAIRR.
A reflective journal, critical discussion and a record of decisions give this process a concrete form.
critique: Examining sources and arguments, distinguishing facts, hypotheses and interpretations, assessing evidence quality and adjusting judgement. It combines reasoning skills with a willingness to question one’s own beliefs.
In scientific reading, teaching and AI use, comparing explanations, their supporting evidence and their limitations.
A critical judgement is reasoned and also considers evidence that challenges initial hypotheses.
mobilisation: Sharing, adapting and co-creating knowledge to support its use in practice and decisions. The process connects knowledge production, users’ needs, ownership, implementation and learning from observed effects.
Adapting courses, public science communication resources and tools to their intended uses, then attending to what is actually used.
Goals and formats vary across professionals, students, citizens and decision-makers. Sharing knowledge is part of an ongoing relationship.
